vision: Corestone is the reader and checker between the field and the design: drop in the drill logs, field sheets, scans, core photos and lab certificates of a campaign, and get back one borehole table where every value is linked to the page it came from, every inconsistency is listed for a geologist to decide, and the logs, sections and exports the firm already uses are drawn from the checked data.

strategy.direction: Own the step between messy field documents and the first borehole table a geologist trusts: read a campaign's field sheets, scanned logs, lab certificates and core photos, check them against each other, and hand back the checked table, every inconsistency with its source, and the exports and drawings the firm already uses. Reading alone is becoming a commodity, so sell the check: start with a free validation report on a firm's own boreholes, price per project or per file, and treat core-photo RQD as one check inside that report rather than as the product.
why: The hours sit in extraction and checking, not modelling: the calls with E4 pains all put the time there, and one design team says interpretation is fast once the data is in its workbook.

The pain repeats across construction and mining in the same shape (PDF in almost every case, lab layouts that break scripts, OCR that turns numbers into letters, QA done by going back to paper), so one engine serves both.

Reading PDF logs is already sold by BoreholeAI, Civils.ai, GeoLayer and Rocscience, which is exactly the '99% already exists' objection; none of them says it checks content across logs, certificates and photos, and UK highway files that pass format validation still fail quality review.
The sharpest error heard, RQD logged at 90% where the photo shows 20%, is a cross-check, not an extraction, and it is what turns a data tool into something a geologist signs against.

Imagery AI is mining-first and consolidating (IMDEX bought Datarock, Seequent owns Imago), so a standalone photo RQD product would meet funded incumbents head on; as a check inside a construction validation report it does not.

The incumbent GI databases are moving users to subscriptions as gINT and HoleBASE support winds down, while small firms on Eng-Tips already say they cannot justify them; per-project pricing fits firms that buy tools, not subscriptions.
A free report on a firm's own data answers the channel problem too: LinkedIn is restricted and cold email got no replies, while the one E5 is a data pack a firm offered to send.

sequence.step: Run the promised drilling-firm data pack and one anonymised design-firm project through reading and the first twenty checks. Measure field-level accuracy, questions per borehole and flags a geologist accepts. Target: two data sets, at least nine values in ten right before questions.

Offer the free validation report to 20 firms from the discovery list (small ground investigation firms and geotechnical teams, Italy and UK first). Deliver 10 reports, debrief each one on the flags, the last campaign's hours and a price per project.
For the three most engaged firms, add exports to their own Excel template, AGS 4 and the Leapfrog CSV set, and one DXF log in their template. Ask for the first paid project.
Test the tender angle cheaply: two calls with estimators at specialist foundation or tunnelling contractors, walking through a lost-money job, before any build.
Decision review against the kill criteria: continue into the certificate reader and photo checks if two firms have paid for a project; otherwise re-plan from the ten debriefs.
If continuing: photo RQD check with the fixed capture rig, archive rescue for exploration consultancies, and the change record for the design handover.

notNow: 3D ground modelling or a Leapfrog substitute: clients in the first market do not pay for 3D models and the established suites own it; export to them instead.
A standalone core-imaging or televiewer product: funded, consolidating incumbents already sell it to mining.
The tender GI check for contractors as a build: no contractor has been interviewed; test it with two calls first.
A shared structural and geotechnical collaboration platform: one voice, a multi-party rollout, and common data environments exist on large projects.
Technical specification generation: a different buyer and a different product.
Seat-based subscriptions: firms buy tools, and per-report or per-file pricing is already the venture's working model.
New industries (construction site documents, energy) before one geotechnical workflow is paid for.
killCriteria: Fewer than nine values in ten read correctly on the first two real data sets after two weeks of tuning: narrow to typed and digital logs before anything else.
Geologists reject more than half of the flags as trivial or wrong: the check does not beat the eye, and the report has nothing to sell.
Fewer than 5 debriefs from 10 delivered reports by 6 November: the report is not a door opener, so change the channel before the product.
No firm pays for a project by 11 January 2027: stop and re-plan from what the debriefs said about budget.
If the debriefs show the firms' own scripts or an existing AI digitiser already catch the same errors, stop building checks and find the next unsolved step.
evidenceGaps: Who pays and from which budget: no price has been discussed in any call. Ask in every report debrief, with a number per project.
Accuracy on real handwriting and scans: unknown until the first data pack is run, due 9 October.
How often the errors change a design parameter, not only a cell: grade every flag in the first ten reports.
Whether UK firms, where AGS files are the norm, feel the extraction pain as much as the Italian and Iberian calls do: book at least three UK conversations by 6 November.
Whether contractors buy a pre-bid ground check: no contractor has been interviewed.
How the AI digitisers perform on the same documents: run one data set through a free pilot of a competitor and compare.
Housekeeping: the compiled VSI ICP and positioning mix in material from other ventures and from public research; recompile them from the calls.

patterns.title: One owner holds the incumbents, and it is moving them to the cloud
patterns.text: Seequent, part of Bentley, owns gINT, HoleBASE, OpenGround, Leapfrog and Imago. gINT support runs to the end of 2028 and users are pointed to OpenGround, whose cloud licences start at published annual prices, while OpenGround Labs adds field-to-lab workflows. Competing databases position on what that move leaves behind: GeoDin on data sovereignty and no tiers, TabLogs on logs per month rather than seats.

evidence.text: gINT support is extended to the end of 2028 on a reasonable endeavour basis, and users are pointed to OpenGround.
OpenGround lists cloud licences at $2,420 a year for i3, with Base and Advanced bundles at $233 and $673 a year.
OpenGround Labs brings field-to-lab workflows and automated test certificates into OpenGround.
GeoDin positions against OpenGround on data sovereignty, with on-premise or private cloud and no credits or tiers.
TabLogs sells cloud boring logs by logs per month, not seats, with published monthly plans.

patterns.title: Reading PDF logs is already a crowded, fast category
patterns.text: BoreholeAI, Civils.ai, GeoLayer, BoreDM and Rocscience all sell AI digitising of borehole logs into AGS and Excel, on speed, formats and volume claims. Extraction alone will not differentiate Corestone; what none of them states is a content check across logs, certificates and photos.

evidence.text: BoreholeAI turns a PDF log into XLSX, AGS, CSV and JSON in under three minutes, with a confidence score per cell.

GeoLayer reads scanned and handwritten logs (depth, strata, SPT, RQD) and exports XLSX, AGS4, gINT, OpenGround and DXF, with a free pilot.
BoreDM combines cloud logging, lab and CPT data, AI digitising of PDF logs, sections and export to Leapfrog.
Rocscience describes an OCR feature in RSLog that digitises paper borehole logs.

Datarock says buyers now ask how the AI fits existing practice rather than whether it works, which favours a check inside an existing workflow over a new tool.

initiatives.title: Log to table: field sheets, scans and logs read into one borehole table
initiatives.summary: Read a batch of handwritten field sheets, scanned logs and digital logs into one borehole table per project, with every value linked to the page and position it came from and every uncertain character asked as a question, then write it into the firm's own Excel template, AGS 4 and the Leapfrog CSV set.
initiatives.bet: We believe that reading a campaign's field sheets and logs into a checked table, with the source of every value one click away, will save engineering geologists the retyping step they all describe as the slowest part of the job. We will know when three firms send a second batch unprompted after the first one comes back.
initiatives.problem: Almost all incoming ground data is PDF or paper; geologists retype it into a master workbook, OCR on scans turns numbers into letters, and QA means going back to the paper to see what the logger wrote.
risks: Accuracy on real handwriting is too low for the table to be trusted, so geologists check every value anyway and save nothing. Measure field-level accuracy on the promised data pack before building anything else.
Firms that already have an Excel and Python chain see this as a small improvement, the hardest objection heard so far. The answer has to be the traced source and the checks, not the typing.
Data sharing needs a manager's approval at design firms, which slows every pilot. Offer to run on anonymised or archive projects first.
The pain is real but the time saved is hard to put a number on, so the price has to be set per project or per file rather than argued from hours.

initiatives.title: Lab certificate reader that does not break when the layout changes
initiatives.summary: Read laboratory and in-situ test certificates (grading, Atterberg limits, CBR, Proctor, triaxial, pressuremeter, UCS) from any lab's PDF or scan into the same table, keeping the raw values and the lab's interpreted ones side by side.
initiatives.bet: We believe that a reader that handles any lab's certificate layout will replace the scripts and OCR that design teams maintain today. We will know when a design team stops maintaining its own parser for one lab it uses often.
initiatives.problem: Every lab issues its own certificate layout, so a parser written for one lab fails on the next and breaks when the lab changes format; there is no European standard for delivering test results.
risks: Tests with curves (pressuremeter, oedometer, triaxial) need more than values read; if the curve is what matters, extraction alone is not enough.
In markets where AGS files are the norm, certificates may already arrive structured, which shrinks the problem there. Check the share of AGS deliveries in the first UK conversations.
Raw lab numbers are rarely disputed, so the value may sit in speed rather than in catching errors.

initiatives.title: Archive rescue: old paper boreholes translated, georeferenced and mapped
initiatives.summary: Read decades-old scanned borehole records in any language, translate descriptions, detect the likely coordinate reference system, flag the ambiguous ones, and place the holes on a map with the rest of the project's data.
initiatives.bet: We believe that turning a box of old paper borehole records into mapped, usable data in days rather than weeks will win exploration and feasibility work where the archive is the first thing a project touches. We will know when one consultancy pays for an archive job.

Resource geologists often exclude historical data because methods changed, which limits the value in mining.
Guessing a coordinate system wrongly is worse than not guessing; every inference must be shown as a question.

initiatives.title: Draft factual report from the checked data
initiatives.summary: Assemble the tables, charts, logs and appendices of a factual ground investigation report from the checked table, in the firm's own structure, leaving interpretation to the geologist.
initiatives.bet: We believe that once the data is trusted, drafting the factual report from it will remove days of assembly on reports of 150 to 200 pages. We will know when a firm edits a Corestone draft rather than starting from its own template.
initiatives.problem: Ground investigation reports run to hundreds of pages and are assembled by hand from tables and charts.
risks: Parked until the table is trusted: a report drafted from unchecked data only moves the errors further down the line.
Report structure varies by firm, client and country, so templating it early is expensive.
Only one team asked for it, and as the end state of a longer chain.
initiatives.firstMove: None for now; revisit when three firms use the validation report on live projects.

initiatives.title: Tender GI check for specialist contractors
initiatives.summary: Read a tender's ground investigation package against public borehole records and a contractor's past jobs, and flag gaps and inconsistencies that would change the price before the bid goes in.
initiatives.bet: We believe that specialist foundation and tunnelling contractors will pay to find ground data gaps before they bid rather than as claims after award. We will know when two contractors send a live tender package to check.
initiatives.problem: Contractors price from the interpretive report in the few weeks a bid allows; inconsistencies surface later on site as claims or losses.
risks: Parked because no contractor has been interviewed: the thesis rests on public tender notices and reasoning, not on a customer conversation.
Bid teams work under deadline and may not take on a new step.
It needs the same reading and checking engine as the validation report, so it can follow it cheaply if the demand appears.
initiatives.firstMove: Book two calls with estimators at specialist foundation or tunnelling contractors and walk through their last lost-money job before building anything for this.

initiatives.title: Light 3D borehole viewer and ground model
initiatives.summary: Place boreholes at their coordinates over topography, correlate them into a simple 3D ground model and overlay a tunnel or pit design to estimate volumes.
initiatives.bet: We believe that a simple 3D view of the boreholes would help firms that cannot justify the established modelling suites. We will know when a client fee pays for a 3D model on a project that would not have had one.
initiatives.problem: Correlating between boreholes is the critical step in modelling, and the established suites are expensive and heavy for small campaigns.
risks: Parked: clients in the first market do not pay for 3D ground models today, so the design team does not even propose them.
The established modelling suites own this and the venture's advisors ruled out building a substitute.
3D interpolation is where errors come from; a light tool could spread them with more confidence than it deserves.
initiatives.firstMove: None for now; exports to the modelling tools firms already use cover the need.
